have revolutionized the field of natural language processing, offering significant improvements in various NLP tasks.  However, the substantial computational resources required to train these models pose a significant challenge.  One promising approach to mitigate this challenge is by utilizing knowledge distillation, a technique where a smaller model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained model.  Knowledge distillation is particularly effective due to its ability to leverage the knowledge embedded in the training data by the pre-trained model, thereby achieving comparable performance with significantly reduced model parameters.  In this paper, we explore the application of knowledge distillation to NLP tasks, examining the efficacy of this method in models like BERT.  Our experiments demonstrate that models trained using knowledge distillation to mimic the behavior of a pre-trained BERT model match the performance of models trained with the BERT model's training data, while requiring a mere 10% of the original model's parameters.  We also analyze the knowledge that the teacher BERT model possesses about the training data, observing that it is directly correlated with the training data.  Interestingly, we find that the student model trained using knowledge distillation is able to mimic the behavior of the teacher model even when the teacher model is trained on a different task, indicating that it is learning the training data's general patterns rather than mere memorization.  In addition, we provide insights into the loss function's design, demonstrating that the temperature parameter has a direct influence on the model's ability to mimic the behavior of the teacher model.  We also offer practical guidelines for selecting the temperature parameter, showing that a value of 4 is optimal for BERT-like models.  In conclusion, our experiments solidify the promise of knowledge distillation in NLP, achieving substantial reductions in model parameters while maintaining comparable performance.  We hope that our findings will enable the wider adoption of this technique in practical settings.  We have implemented our approach in an open-source repository, accessible via this link.  Through this work, we aim to facilitate further research and applications of knowledge distillation in NLP.  In particular, we explore multi-task learning as an exciting direction for future study, a phenomenon where a model is trained on multiple tasks simultaneously.  In this case, we propose that knowledge distillation could enable a model to learn multiple tasks with a single teacher model, thereby opening up new avenues for collaborative learning in NLP.  We have discussed this idea with peers and have plans to investigate this direction further.  We have also collaboratively initiated a discussion thread

Despite significant research, accurately translating implicit meaning, particularly in figurative language, remains a persistent challenge.  This study focuses on translating idioms, which are expressions with non-literal meaning, from English to Spanish.  First, we define an Ixon (Idiom eXtraction and ONset) dataset containing 5,000 English sentences, including 200 unique idioms not previously analyzed.  Next, in an Ixon MT evaluation framework, we assess the performance of existing MT systems on translating these idioms and surrounding context.  Our results reveal that current MT systems struggle to capture the non-literal meaning of idioms, with only 34% accuracy in understanding the original meaning and 41% accuracy in reproducing it.  However, we find that incorporating a technique aimed at identifying latent meanings can enhance the translation quality for these idioms, indicating a potential approach to improving MT performance on complex linguistic constructs.  This work provides essential steps towards developing more effective MT systems capable of handling figurative language, with the Ixon dataset serving as a resource for future research and evaluation. This issue stems from the complexity involved in implementing accurate and efficient algorithms for sampling continuous and discrete probability distributions, as well as propagating uncertainties through analytical or numerical methods.  Our project addresses this gap by providing an intuitive and versatile simulation toolkit that allows users to easily set up and execute a wide range of simulations for continuous and discrete distributions, including novel applications such as matrix-valued scenarios.  This toolkit also includes innovative efficient algorithms for common scenarios and utilizes multiple numerical libraries to handle more complex tasks, while being accessible across various platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS.  We have also developed an interactive simulation dashboard and an online platform to showcase the results of our project, featuring simulations for over a hundred different scenarios and allowing users to explore and customize their own setups.  This project represents a crucial step towards creating a comprehensive simulation toolkit that can be adapted to meet the testing needs of diverse scientific applications.  To this end, we welcome feedback and suggestions from users and potential collaborators, while also opening up our project's source code and data to the research community on a collaborative platform.  We have also incorporated an ongoing survey initiative on this platform, where researchers and industry professionals can share their simulation requirements and proposed solutions can be posted as potential collaborations or project submissions for academic conferences and job positions.  This survey initiative will be updated regularly and its results will be presented as a report, to ultimately contribute to the ongoing development and refinement of our simulation toolkit and to promote the adoption of simulation testing best practices across various disciplines. This paper introduces a non-parametric method to estimate extreme quantile regressions when the underlying data distribution is unknown and heavy-tailed.  Based on this estimate, new tests are created to determine if specific variables influence outcomes more than expected in a heavy-tailed world.  Using simulated data and the stock price volatility of small firms as an example, this paper demonstrates the effectiveness of these tests.  It also finds that, unlike in a normal distribution setting, the new tests do not suffer from size diffusion and maintain similar power compared to their normal distribution counterparts.  Additionally, the paper analyzes the performance of the new estimate and compares it to the normal distribution estimate in a heavy-tailed environment, finding that the new estimate outperforms the normal distribution estimate in terms of bias and root mean squared error.  Furthermore, the paper provides recommendations for selecting the tuning parameter in the new estimate, suggesting that it is more robust when data is sparse.  Finally, the paper provides a proxy for heavy-tailed data that can be used as input for the new estimate, showing that this proxy is robust when data includes outliers.  Using US inflation data as an example, the paper also demonstrates the applicability of the new estimate and tests to study the persistence of heavy-tailed phenomena in economics.  Additionally, the paper provides a dataset that combines multiple datasets from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) and allows researchers to replicate the results mentioned in the paper.  Moreover, the paper introduces a new R package called qrglm that extends the generalised linear model to extreme quantile regression and enables researchers to estimate heavy-tailed outcomes using multiple distributions such as Cauchy and Laplace.  This package provides a user-friendly interface for selecting the tuning parameter in the new estimate and includes multiple methods such as least squares and minimum distance method to estimate extreme quantile regressions.  This package also introduces a new test called the wild score test that enables researchers to test the significance of coefficients in extreme quantile regressions.  This package further provides results in table and figure formats that enable visual comparison of the new estimate and the normal distribution estimate.  This package also provides data demonstration that enables researchers to replicate the results mentioned in the paper using US inflation data and provides example code that enables researchers to estimate extreme quantile regressions using the new estimate and the normal distribution estimate.  This package is compatible with Windows, macOS and Unix systems and can be installed using the base R package

peptide barriers are now intensely researched, particularly in relation to their connection to galactic magnetic fields.  A recently observed peak in the Barnard 68 region has sparked renewed interest in measuring the kinetic temperature of gas.  Temperature measurements are crucial to determine the barrier strength and thus evaluate the impact of magnetic fields, which induce a temperature restriction and prevent gas from escaping into the surrounding interstellar medium.  However, existing models based on molecular line widths have limitations, primarily due to contamination and opacities affecting data interpretation.  To overcome these challenges, observations of the N2H+ line with high angular resolution allowed us to measure line widths independently of opacities and contamination, yielding a temperature measurement of approximately 8 K.  Consequently, the barrier strength in this region is sufficiently low to explain the observed peak, and thus it is unlikely due to magnetic pressure.  Instead, it is more likely the result of a density increase in this particular region.  In order to confirm this finding, it is necessary to measure the kinetic temperature in other peptide barrier locations, which in turn will allow us to determine density increases and thus better comprehend the formation of density enhancements in the outer regions of star-forming cores.  To this end, we propose a survey of the 1.4 GHz N2H+ line with high angular resolution across the CoKern sample, which includes the Barnard 68 region, with the ultimate goal of determining line widths and thus kinetic temperatures.  Consequently, we will be able to determine density increases and peptide barrier strengths, which in turn will allow us to evaluate the impact of magnetic fields on density enhancements and peptide barrier strengths, and thus matter circulation in the interstellar medium, which is influenced by the breakdown of peptide barriers, on the formation of stars. In this study, we explore the concept of list coloring, which involves assigning sets of colors, known as lists, to the vertices of a graph. Each list contains colors that can be used to color the corresponding vertex. If we can choose one color from each list such that the graph's edges satisfy the usual coloring condition, we call this choice an acceptable coloring. obstructions within non-destructive testing images is an ongoing challenge in various industries, including aerospace and energy.  This study introduces a novel, self-contained method for detecting anomalies within NDT images by leveraging their translation-invariant structure.  By combining a correlation-based image matching technique with a robust method for determining the anomaly location, this approach can identify anomalies even in images that have been distorted by the presence of obstacles.  Key benefits of this method include its ability to handle distorted images, reduce false positives, and provide accurate location of anomalies with minimal adjustment.  Comparing algorithms for determining the anomaly location, including one with an intuitive mathematical foundation, demonstrates that an energy-based approach yields the best results.  Furthermore, a classification system that identifies images with anomalies from a general NDT image dataset shows high accuracy.  With minimal tuning, this system detects anomalies in NDT images with high precision and accuracy.  Finally, a proposed application for this method involves using deep learning to enhance NDT images, which in turn enables the detection of anomalies with even higher precision.  Code and data for this research are available at https://github.com/22amar/amar-22. The proposed technique leverages the structural invariance inherent in NDT images to identify anomalies even in images distorted by physical obstacles.  With the ability to handle distorted images, our method reduces false positives and accurately pinpoints anomaly locations with minimal adjustment.  We compared various methods for determining optimal windows, including one with a mathematical foundation, and found that the projection operator approach yields best results.  A classification system that identifies images containing anomalies from a general NDT image dataset shows high accuracy.  With minimal tuning, our system detects anomalies in NDT images with high precision and accuracy.  As an application, we explored using this method in conjunction with a deep learning based image enhancement technique to enhance NDT images and improve anomaly detection. This research reexamines the effectiveness of such methods by analyzing their representation learning mechanisms.  It argues that, in supervised learning, only neighboring samples that share the same class label can be considered similar enough to be compared using a contrastive objective.  To increase the method's generalization, the number of neighboring samples should be limited to reduce overfitting.  Based on this analysis, a new supervised learning framework called Supervised Contrastive Learning is proposed.  It separates the dataset into two parts: a main batch consisting of the input image and a few positively-sampled neighbors with the same class label, and a surrounding batch generated from the remaining images in the dataset.  The model minimizes the representation difference between the main batch and surrounding batch using a contrastive objective, which is adapted into two separate prediction tasks with different temperatures.  A simple but effective method that generates positive neighbors is also introduced.  Experimental results show that Supervised Contrastive Learning outperforms previous supervised learning methods and achieves comparable performance to classification methods using the ResNet-50 backbone on the CIFAR-10, Flowers, and Pet datasets.  Moreover, it exhibits robust performance when varying the number of positive neighbors.  In unsupervised learning scenarios, adding a momentum term to the Contrastive Multiview Learning method enhances the model's generalization, which is verified by comparing the results of different supervised and unsupervised learning frameworks. As such, ensuring the reliability of these models in these domains is increasingly crucial. Model-3 accuracy, which measures the degree to which a model predicts its own accurate performance, has been proposed as a solution to this problem. In our research, we examine the notion of model accuracy and propose a framework to help developers create datasets for training models that are self-aware of their own accuracy. We also include a publicly accessible resource containing data sets for various image classification models, along with their corresponding performance metrics. As shown in experiments, this approach enables the development of more reliable models through self-awareness, reducing the cost associated with labeling large data sets. Furthermore, our framework accelerates the development of robust models by identifying key factors that influence their performance and can be used to identify models prone to security vulnerabilities. As demonstrated, the model-3 accuracy concept has significant practical implications, given the significant economic benefits of using computer vision models in industrial and healthcare settings. In conclusion, the introduction of model-3 accuracy marks a significant step towards creating trustworthy computer vision models, and researchers and practitioners are encouraged to build upon this concept, exploring its applications in other model types and problem domains.

In reality, people have distinct cultural backgrounds that significantly influence their perceptions and behaviors.  Given the importance of culture in personalization, a revised approach is needed that takes it into consideration.  Currently, collecting cultural data in a supervised setting is challenging because it requires labeling a broad range of cultural attributes. A study submitted in this abstract investigates 11 of these events which took place between 2019 and 2021 and were detected by the Newton X-ray telescope on board the e-ASTROSat during observations of the Hubble Deep Field South.  Using these observations and accompanying data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, XMM-Newton, and the Swift X-ray Telescope, the findings reveal the transients emit most of their X-ray energy in the 0.3-10 keV range and have intrinsic spectra similar to that of active galactic nuclei.  A statistical analysis of the data from these 11 events also provided a rough estimate of the transient rate density, suggesting there may be over 200 of these events per year in the Hubble Deep Field South.  Furthermore, the detected transients were all located at redshifts less than 2.5, with some as close as 1.1 billion light-years from Earth, and exhibited no apparent association with host galaxies in deep optical and near-infrared images.  Follow-up observations with the e-ASTROSat revealed two of the transients still active days to weeks after their initial detection, suggesting they may be linked to compact remnants of massive stars accreting material from their surroundings.  A potential candidate for a transient detected by the e-ASTROSat prior to its targeted observations is also discussed, along with the implications of these discoveries for the multi-messenger study of these enigmatic events.  Ultimately, the detection of these transients and the opportunities they present for further study and the multi-messenger community are significant, however, the lack of a dedicated alert system for the e-ASTROSat poses a limitation.  An alert system like this would enable rapid follow-up observations and the collection of detailed data on these fleeting events, increasing the potential for their study and the chances of detecting them across the full field of view of the e-ASTROSat's X-ray telescope.  An algorithm for detecting these transients and triggering follow-up observations is currently being developed using the e-ASTROSat's onboard software, which will enable the detection of transients in real-time and facilitate fast follow-up observations with the remaining pointing positions of the spacecraft. This kind of misinformation poses a public health threat by causing people to adopt ineffective prevention measures, leading to a decrease in vaccination uptake, and resulting in delayed medical care seeking behavior. 

  As a potential solution, we analyzed Twitter data from June to July 2020 to investigate the feasibility of using conversational language to identify and correct COVID-19-related misinformation. We utilized a dataset containing 328,000 Twitter posts annotated by humans to develop a multi-step framework. 

  Initially, we used a two-class classifier to distinguish between posts containing COVID-19-related misinformation and those that do not. Subsequently, we employed a method to pinpoint the misleading information within positive samples. Next, we developed a model to identify the effective language needed to correct the misinformation. Finally, we combined the corrected language with the extracted misinformation to form correction responses.

  Our models achieved high accuracy in classifying posts containing misinformation and accurately identified the misinformation within positive samples as well as developed language for correction. Based on these results, we propose a Twitter-based health misinformation correction framework that involves conversational language. 

  As a further contribution, we open-source our code and make our dataset available for public use.

We propose statistically robust and computationally efficient methods for estimating options prices using our Option LP framework. Through sparse regression, we improve estimation accuracy by reducing overfitting. Our results outperform the Black-Scholes model in scenarios representative of real-world applications, and excel in scenarios characterized by non-consant options prices, multiple factors influencing options prices, and limited availability of large datasets. Our code is freely available and can be used with the ROPtools library.  We also introduce an open dataset containing prices of European options computed using the Black-Scholes model, along with other related data, which is available on the QuantPlatform repository.  Finally, we highlight several potential directions for further research and applications of our methods.  Options prices estimation is a key component in derivative instruments risk management. However, due to the complex nature of options prices, and the large number of parameters involved, it is not possible to determine an exact options prices formula. As a result, practitioners resort to using approximate methods, such as the Black-Scholes model, which assumes constant options prices and specific distribution parameters, and estimates options prices through closed-form expressions. Person Re-ID) aims to link the same person across non-overlapping camera views without using identity labels. It has important applications in surveillance and intelligence systems. However, the challenging task is hindered by poor quality images, incorrect annotations, and limited training data. This paper addresses these issues with a novel method that utilizes unsupervised domain adaptation and cross-camera view data. First, it extracts a person code from each image, representing visual features. The proposed framework leverages a domain confusion technique to discover and discard incorrect annotations, preventing them from influencing the mapping function. Additionally, it exploits a contrastive learning strategy to update the person code and mapping function simultaneously, ensuring they work in tandem. This paper investigates the application of ensemble techniques to medical image segmentation tasks. It demonstrates the efficacy of these techniques, which not only enhance prediction accuracy but also produce more reliable confidence scores.  The code and models used here can be applied to a wide range of tasks and datasets.  As an example, we showcase their application to brain and liver segmentation using publicly available datasets.  We believe that using ensemble methods yields more consistent results and better metric optimization.  These benefits come with the added advantage of reduced model dependence, which is critical in medical image analysis.  It is worth noting that while ensemble methods do increase model complexity and computational requirements, our results demonstrate the practicality of these techniques in real-world medical image segmentation projects.  As an additional contribution, we release a metric stability tool that assesses the reliability of model predictions.  This tool can be used to filter ensemble models with unstable predictions and select only those with high metric scores.  We showcase the application and effectiveness of this tool in model selection, which is essential in medical image analysis.  As an example, we use it to identify liver segmentation models with high DSC scores and stable predictions.  The code and models used here can be found at the specified URL. As an example, we successfully used these techniques in brain and prostate segmentation, but the associated models are currently being optimized and will be shared later. Eventually, we aim to release this tool as an open repository, which will enable other researchers to use it and leverage our ensemble models.
